Now, here are 4 news stories that broke in the morning to watch out for:
Producer Price Index rises 0.4% in August:

0.4% month-over-month in August, matching consensus estimates, with the year-over-year reading coming in at 5.4%. The index for final demand goods advanced 1.1% following two consecutive declines, while services prices rose 0.1% for a third straight month. Core PPI, excluding food and energy, came in slightly below expectations at 0.2% versus 0.3% forecast. Analysts pointed to rising diesel costs—now nearly $6 a gallon—as a key risk for inflation in the coming months, with oil back above $100 a barrel adding pressure on input costs across the economy.

The benchmark 10-year yield rose 5 basis points to 4.90%, a peak not seen since November 2023, while the 30-year yield advanced 5 basis points to 5.34%—matching levels last recorded in June 2007 and marking a 19-year high for the long bond. Traders viewed the data as confirmation that wholesale price pressures have not faded enough to alter the Federal Reserve's policy outlook.
Copper stocks tumble on White House tariff delay:

Copper miners  plunged  after Reuters reported the Trump administration has not yet decided on refined copper import tariffs, weighing concerns over higher manufacturing costs against potential benefits for domestic mining. Freeport-McMoRan dropped 8.2%, Hudbay Minerals fell 6.9%, and Southern Copper declined 6.4%. Benchmark copper on the London Metal Exchange traded down 3% to $14,329.50 per metric ton after earlier touching a record high of $14,875 per ton. Analysts warned of bubble risk, noting prices are being driven by U.S. import arbitrage opportunities rather than end-consumer demand.
Federal court rejects bid to block cannabis rescheduling:

A federal appeals court  denied a motion by opponents seeking to halt the Trump administration's plan to move medical marijuana from Schedule I to Schedule III under the Controlled Substances Act. The challengers, including the National Drug and Alcohol Screening Association, argued that marijuana abuse has consequences and that tax benefits for cannabis companies would increase sales and abuse. The Justice Department countered that the attempt was motivated by "pocketbook interests served by keeping all marijuana in Schedule I."
